📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fiona first rose to fame when she was born premature at Cincinnati Zoo in 2017.

Major League Soccer side FC Cincinnati will honour Fiona, a hippo that recently died at the city's zoo, with a tifo display at their match with Nashville SC on Saturday.

Fiona, a social media star since her premature birth at the zoo in 2017, died on Thursday after swallowing a woollen hat that had slipped into her enclosure.

The Ohio side will now raise a banner depicting the nine-year-old semi-aquatic mammal in their post-season MLS Cup encounter with Nashville, who won the Supporters' Shield for being the highest-placed team in the league campaign.

Cincinnati said Fiona was a "beloved hippo who became a symbol of Cincinnati and captured hearts around the world".

The tifo will be produced by fan group The Forge Cincy, who painted the display on Sunday in a garage next to Cincinnati's TQL Stadium.

The club will also make a donation in Fiona's memory for every fan in attendance to the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden.

Fan group The Forge Cincy had previously spent two weeks creating a tifo for their "Hell is Real" October derby match against Ohio rivals Columbus.

Removal of hat inside Fiona the hippo was 'impossible', Cincinnati Zoo claims.

Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo.

Cincinnati's Nick Hagglund, who hails from the city and is in his eighth season with the team, previously paid tribute to Fiona after scoring in his side's 3-1 victory over Orlando on the day of her death.

The defender yelled "that's for Fiona", mimicking the ears on top of her head, in a celebration video, external on the club's Instagram.

Later, on his Instagram account, external, Hagglund posted, "This one was for her @fionahippo @cincinnatizoo.

"Cincinnati needed a win on the day after the passing of our beloved hippo, a symbol of hope and resilience for our city, and the lads answered the call.".

Cincinnati's tifo is one of a number of tributes paid to the hippo, with Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Tee Higgins wearing a Fiona sweater, external prior to his American football franchise's defeat by the Washington Commanders on Monday.

Meanwhile handlers of the blue hippo balloon at New York's annual Macy's Thanksgiving Parade will wear a purple patch in her honour.

At birth, Fiona weighed 13kg (29lb), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species, and she previously inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.

From premature baby to social media star - famed Cincinnati Zoo hippo Fiona dies.

Fiona swallowed the woollen hat around 10 days prior to her death, with the item getting into her enclosure by accident after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.

Hippos normally live up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo.

Nashville finished top of the MLS Eastern Conference, 31 points ahead of ninth-placed Cincinnati.

However, having beaten Orlando in a one-off wildcard round, Cincinnati defeated Nashville 1-0 in the opening match of their best-of-three round one series.

Should Cincinnati win on Saturday they will progress to a one-off conference semi-final with either Chicago Fire or Charlotte FC, with a conference final prior to the season-ending MLS Cup final.

#162214. Newly introduced discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Newly introduced discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (984 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency.
  • Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an notable clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature.
  • To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an notable clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising latest direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold.

According to recent reports, superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

In a recent development, superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an vital advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

Sources indicate that "We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.".

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature.

The upcoming study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," notes Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.".

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together.

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

Sources indicate that an analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In a recent development, in conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

It has been revealed that "The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," indicates Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.".

In a recent development, phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.".

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue.

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

It has been revealed that unlike conventional measurement approaches, the upcoming instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

#162213. Tech Report: Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

Tech Report: Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty.
  • It has been revealed that A new study suggests they become more likely to follow.
  • They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

It has been revealed that A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group.".

The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

Recent findings suggest that small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

According to recent reports, good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

According to recent reports, people were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Sources indicate that not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

Sources indicate that to see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

It has been revealed that in some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

Industry observers note that molleman calls the work fundamental science and claims the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

Sources indicate that he also states it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.".

Kevin de Bruyne won 16 trophies in 10 years at Manchester City.

Kevin de Bruyne's move to Napoli in 2025 was supposed to mark a continuation of his glittering decade at Manchester City as he approaches the twilight years of his career.

Instead, the midfielder, who is widely regarded as one of the standout players of his generation, has seen his time in Naples threaten to turn sour amid an early injury, friction with his team-mates and rumours of a January exit.

Napoli were Serie A champions in 2024-25 - the year before De Bruyne's arrival - but are right now languishing in eighth, while they sit 27th in the Champions League after a heavy 4-1 defeat at Porto earlier this month.

Belgium international De Bruyne lifted 16 trophies in his 10 years at City and is guaranteed a generous ovation when he returns to the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday but the highs of his time in England are in contrast to the struggles he is seemingly enduring in Italy.

"Not a lot I can say for the moment," mentioned De Bruyne when asked about his future. "I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

"There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.".

De Bruyne's feelings for Man City will 'never change'.

Did Man City let De Bruyne leave too soon?

Statue, Pep's tears & a missed sitter - De Bruyne's emotional farewell.

City decided not to renew De Bruyne's contract during the 2024-25 season and the player had the choice of heading to the US with Chicago Fire or staying in one of the top-five leagues in Europe.

The 35-year-old felt he could still cut it at the highest level but his first season at Napoli was heavily disrupted by a hamstring injury which kept him out for more than four months, restricting him to 21 appearances.

Napoli finished runners up to Inter Milan to lose their Serie A title and De Bruyne reportedly said, external he was "happy" manager Antonio Conte had departed in the summer as promises were not kept regarding the style of play.

But despite making his name as a technically gifted number 10, De Bruyne's role has been remodelled into a deeper holding one under Massimiliano Allegri in an ageing squad that has struggled this season.

In Porto, the fractures were clear to see, with De Bruyne having a heated on-field confrontation, external with striker Lorenzo Lucca and his team-mates were forced to step in to diffuse the situation.

The passionate side of De Bruyne's game was shown in Manchester too.

The midfielder shouted "shut up" at manager Pep Guardiola during a Champions League game against Real Madrid in 2023, and said "let me talk" when David Silva and Fernandinho were ushering him off the pitch at half-time shortly after he was booked against Napoli in 2017.

"Speaking about the pitch, De Bruyne is the best player this year at Napoli," Naples-based journalist Vincenzo Credendino tells BBC Sport. "The point is that the whole team is having difficulties.

Recent findings suggest that "We saw that there is a problem, at least between De Bruyne and Lorenzo Lucca. Their acting was very, very clear and I think that in that time, the two of them were wrong.

"On one hand you cannot swear at another team-mate but on the other hand, De Bruyne reproached Lucca without encouraging him, so it was a bad show.".

De Bruyne has played 16 times for Napoli this season - contributing four goals and two assists - but his long-term future at the club remains unclear.

In September, De Bruyne's wife reportedly, external told a Belgian publication about their desire to move back home, saying "the sooner we get there, the better" as the player leads a "very restricted life" in Naples.

Asked if the quotes had been misinterpreted, De Bruyne stated: "To be honest, I am pretty annoyed because if you read the article, that none of you have read, to understand what she said.

"I was away in Belgium and a lot of noise came and a lot of bad reactions to my wife and family. I saw pictures of my house, I don't think it is OK but it is what it is and some press created this in Italy. I don't know why.

According to recent reports, "Nobody knows my life, you will never know. People who work with me are not allowed to say anything but obviously it is something that I take away and think about. It has not been nice for my wife or for my family.".

It has led to interest from the Netherlands with PSV Eindhoven making a Â£1.67m offer to sign him in January, but the two clubs are apart in their valuations as Napoli want up to Â£6.7m, according to Credendino.

"Napoli fans were not happy [with the interview]," he says. "There are many fans that say, 'OK, you can leave if you want, we are not putting chains on anybody'.".

Napoli boss Allegri left the door open for a January exit by saying in his pre-match news conference the pair had "not spoken" about his future and it is "down to the players and who wants to leave" when the transfer window opens.

City manager Enzo Maresca was assistant to Pep Guardiola during the 2022-23 campaign in which De Bruyne helped the club to a Treble of trophies and the Italian has fond memories of the "fantastic season" they spent together.

It has been revealed that "No doubt, [he is] one of the best," Maresca said of De Bruyne in his pre-match news conference. "Not only personally but also for the history of this club. In the last 10 years all the trophies the club achieved Kevin was here.

"He was an vital player, a top guy, polite and for me it was a pleasure to work with him.".

This is not the first time De Bruyne will be facing his former club with a reunion with City in the Champions League last season.

That trip turned out to be a bitterly unhappy experience, with De Bruyne substituted after 26 minutes following Giovanni di Lorenzo's red card in the 2-0 defeat.

The midfielder will be hoping for a better result on Tuesday as he aims to park his struggles for one evening.

City and Belgium winger Jeremy Doku said: "Kevin is someone that likes football. Even at this age he loves it.

"I don't have any doubts about his quality and I am sure everything will be fine in Napoli.".

#162209. Seth Rogen Reveals “Bad Dynamic” on Dawson’s Creek During Guest Role

Seth Rogen Reveals “Bad Dynamic” on Dawson’s Creek During Guest Role

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eonline

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Studio star admitted that he had a less than stellar time guest starring on Dawson’s Creek in 2003, adding he felt some tensions among the cast and crew.
  • In a recent development, “I hated that,” Rogen confessed on the Nov.
  • The 44-year-old explained that he was convinced to appear on the season six episode “Rock Bottom” by his former Freaks and Geeks costar and Dawson’s Creek actress Busy Philipps after she appeared on his show Undeclared.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seth Rogen couldn’t wait for this gig to be over.

The Studio star admitted that he had a less than stellar time guest starring on Dawson’s Creek in 2003, adding he felt some tensions among the cast and crew.

In a recent development, “I hated that,” Rogen confessed on the Nov. 16 episode of the Happy Sad Confused podcast. “That was not fun.”.

The 44-year-old explained that he was convinced to appear on the season six episode “Rock Bottom” by his former Freaks and Geeks costar and Dawson’s Creek actress Busy Philipps after she appeared on his show Undeclared.

“She was like, ‘Hey, now that I’m doing this, you gotta do Dawson’s Creek.’ And I was like, ‘Haha,’” Rogen recalled. “And then, like, six months later, I’m on the set of Dawson’s Creek. I was like, ‘How did this happen?’”.

And according to the Emmy winner, the drama wasn’t just onscreen, as he revealed there was plenty behind-the-scenes, too.

“It was so weird,” he shared. “And there was a lot of resentment between, like, the showrunners and the cast—it was a very bad dynamic.”.

He had quite a harrowing experience away from the set, too, adding, “I was staying in, like, a haunted hotel and had a nervous breakdown.”.

E! News has reached out to Dawson’s Creek creator Kevin Williamson, as well as showrunners Greg Berlanti and Tom Kapinos for comment but has not heard back.

Kapinos previously expressed his own frustration with the series that ran from 1998 to 2003 and starred the late James Van Der Beek, Katie Holmes, Joshua Jackson and Michelle Williams.

Sources indicate that "The experience was miserable," he shared during a 2009 Emmys panel. "But it was a four-year boot camp. It was like going to TV grad school and learning how to run a television show. Anybody on that show who could make a decision was allowed to run it at some point. I inherited the very awkward college years, and I almost ran the show into the ground. But I learned everything that I needed to know about how to run a show.".

Still, he was far from the only resident of the Creek who had problems during the series, as Williams explained being on the show for so long deterred her from doing television for a number of years as she feared a “loss of input.”.

As Williams explained, being on the show for so long deterred her from doing television for a number of years as she feared a “loss of input.”.

Sources indicate that “Doing Dawson’s Creek for six-and-a-half years, while it was an incredible learning experience—we did 22 episodes a year, and you’d be getting scripts at the last minute and you had zero input,” she shared with actress Patricia Clarkson during an interview for Variety in 2019. “It was a little like a factory job. It was formulaic.”.

For more secrets from the set of Dawson’s Creek, keep reading.

While Fox was first to pick up Dawson's Creek, it subsequently dumped the teen drama.

"I was told they were struggling with Party of Five and they didn't need another one," series creator Kevin Williamson said at the 2015 ATX TV Festival.

But that paved the way for The WB to pick it up two years later.

While Paula Cole's "I Don't Want to Wait" became the iconic Dawson's Creek theme song, producers originally wanted Alanis Morissette's "Hand in My Pocket.".

Alas, they couldn't land the rights, what a jagged little pill.

Dawson. Pacey. Joey. Not names you hear every day. So how did Williamson come up with them?

"Dawson came from a real place called Dawson's Creek where we all hung out as kids and partied," he told The Hollywood Reporter in 2018, while Pacey "came from a friend of a friend named Pacey and I'd never met anyone with that name and thought it was a cool name.".

And for the show's heroine, Williamson "wanted Josephine as a very girly name that could easily turn into a tomboy name like Joey.".

Remember Dawson's infamous "walk the dog" line in the pilot?

Williamson inserted the euphemism because the network would not let them say the word "masturbate" in 1998.

Before Katie Holmes was cast in the role that would make her America's sweetheart-next-door, Blair was this close to landing the role.

"Joe was written to be a tomboy and everyone was coming in being very much a tomboy. We were very close to going with Selma Blair, who was amazing," Williamson told THR. "She read it very tough, with a lot of heart.".

However, once he saw Holmes on tape, with "those two big eyes," Williamson knew they had their Joey.

Joshua Jackson Was Almost Dawson.

Williamson liked Joshua Jackson so much, he didn't care what role the Mighty Ducks alum played.

Industry observers note that "I fell in love with Josh Jackson because he could read any role, Dawson or Pacey," he told THR. "But something wasn't complete and that's when the network remarked they didn't see Josh as Dawson, and rightfully so. So, I went, 'OK, he's Pacey,' because I knew I wanted him in the show no matter what.".

Charlie Hunnam Auditioned, Won Role of Husband.

An 18-year-old Charlie Hunnam read for the WB drama in 1999 and, while he didn't land the part, he did meet Katherine Towne at his audition.

They tied the knot in Las Vegas three weeks later and divorced in 2002, "three terrible, painful, expensive years later," as Hunnam put it to the Associated Press in 2017.

Dawson's Creek became so popular that American Eagle inked a deal in 2000 to outfit the actors.

The characters wore mostly AE clothes throughout season three, and the cast appeared in ad campaigns and promos for the clothing line, helping drive the company's net income above $105 million in 2001.

When James Van Der Beek was first cast, the studio wanted him to change his hair.

"We found an ad for The Devil's Own, the movie with Brad Pitt," he recalled to The Daily Beast in 2012. "They noted: 'What about Brad Pitt's haircut?' That's how I got my season one haircut.".

Joey and Pacey's Real-Life Love.

Holmes dated Jackson early in the show's run, before Pacey and Joey realized they opposite-of-hated each other.

"I'm just going to say that I met somebody last year," Holmes told Rolling Stone in 1998, not denying that the somebody was Jackson. "I fell in love, I had my first love, and it was something so incredible and indescribable that I will treasure it always. And that I feel so fortunate because he's now one of my best friends. It's weird, it's almost like a Dawson-and-Joey type thing now.".

It has been revealed that plus one more nugget: "He's been in the business so long," she added, "and he's really helped me. I respect him as a friend and a professional.".

Kerr Smith Didn't Know Jack Was Gay.

When Kerr Smith first signed on to join the show as Joey's new boyfriend, he had no idea the character would eventually come out and be part of the first-ever gay kiss on TV.

In a recent development, "I always knew I wanted Jack to come out of the closet, but I didn't even tell [Smith]," Williamson noted at the ATX TV Festival. "Let the audience love him, then let's have him come out of the closet and have Joey have to deal with that—and then that would eventually drive her back to [Dawson].".

More poignantly, Williamson has remarked that every character on the show inherited traits from him, including Jack.

“Every single character has a trait of me in them,” he told Entertainment Weekly in 2018. “I had just, in my 20s, gone through the coming-out process and had told my parents I was gay. I had taken that whole journey, and I wanted a character on the show to represent that journey and to represent that side of me.".

Jack's coming out episode, cowritten by Williamson and producer Greg Berlanti, was inspired by true events.

"A friend of mine had a story that I brought in that he got outed accidentally," Berlanti told EW, "because he wrote a love poem that it was so clear to everyone else that it was about a guy.”.

Michelle Williams and Busy Philipps' best-friendship, which first blossomed on Dawson's Creek, is still going strong to this day.

It has been revealed that “I’m so in love with her,” Williams told People of her bestie at a 2016 screening of Manchester by the Sea, one of many red carpet date nights for the besties. “She’s proof that the love of your life does not have to be a man! That’s the love of my life right there.”.

Philipps is also godmother to Williams' daughter Matilda Ledger, who was born in 2005.

Dawson finally losing his virginity was such a significant show moment that Van Der Beek brought a very special gift to set the day the scene was filmed.

"I remember bringing champagne for the crew—Dawson finally lost his virginity!" he told The Daily Beast.

Chad Michael Murray, One Tree Heel?

Before starring on One Tree Hill, Chad Michael Murray had an arc on Dawson's Creek playing Charlie, a love interest for Jen and Joey.

But while Charlie got around, Murray didn't seem to make a lot of friends during his first stint in North Carolinav (OTH later filmed there).

During a Paley panel in 2009, Philipps called him "a douche," later saying, "Don't worry. I'm not real worried about burning bridges with CMM.".

It has been revealed that van Der Beek added, "He's actually come a long way." Post-event, Philipps tweeted, "Just finished the dawson's creek panel. Maybe I was too harsh on chadM2… Nah.".

Murray, meanwhile, hasn't stirred the pot, saying in 2015 that he learned a lot from the experience.

“I had the opportunity to learn from people who had been doing it for a couple of years longer than I was when I walked into the Dawson’s cast,” he told Cosmpolitan.com in 2015. “You know, Michelle and James and Katie and Josh—they really kind of guided me, because they’d already been around for five, six years, maybe longer. And if they had the time, they were showing me the ropes. I had no idea what lighting was, I had no idea about a lot of the technical aspects of what we do, and so I’m grateful for that experience.”.

Just a sampling of the famous faces, ranging from the already familiar to future huge stars, who appeared on Dawson's Creek over the years: Seth Rogen, Jane Lynch, Julie Bowen, Scott Foley, Jensen Ackles, Hilarie Burton, Rachel Leigh Cook, Ali Larter and Oliver Hudson.

Young Americans was a short-lived spinoff centering on Pacey's friend Will Krudski (Rodney Scott) and his boarding school classmates at Rawley Academy.

Also starring Ian Somerhalder and Kate Bosworth, it was canceled after just one season.

The Show Almost Ended With Joey Picking Dawson.

The show's main love triangle officially disassembled when Joey chose Pacey in the 2003 series finale.

According to recent reports, but it almost didn't turn out that way, as Williamson first envisioned Dawson getting the girl. But halfway through writing the finale, Williamson realized that a happy ending for that couple wasn't "what the show was set to be.".

"I wanted it to be a twist on the teen genre but also wanted it to be surprising, honest and real and say something about soul mates and what soul mates can be," he explained at the ATX TV Festival. "That's why we did it that way. When you left the show in that last moment, they're a family and everyone got what they wanted. There was fulfillment and they were all happy.".

At the last minute, he changed his mind and the rest is TV history. But Williamson admitted his mom, who played for Team Dawson, was not happy.

In the finale, which jumped ahead five years, the group had to deal with the devastating loss of Jen.

According to recent reports, "Dealing with the death of one of their own was the final thing that thrust them into adulthood forever. Dawson's Creek was a coming-of-age story and that was the idea behind that ending," Williamson explained of the decision. "That's why we killed Jen, because I wanted them to deal with a death of one their own as that final lesson.".

Some of the executive producers who get their start on Dawson's?

Julie Plec (who went on to gift us with The Vampire Diaries and The Originals), Berlanti (Everwood, Arrow, The Flash, Riverdale...the list goes on and on, and that doesn't even include his movies), Rob Thomas (Veronica Mars and iZombie), Jenny Bicks (Sex and the City), Anna Fricke (Being Human), Dana Baratta (Jessica Jones) and many more.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A Premier League trophy and 21 goals in his debut season - on paper things have worked out perfectly for Viktor Gyokeres since his Â£64m transfer to Arsenal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Viktor Gyokeres has scored twice in all competitions this season.

A Premier League trophy and 21 goals in his debut season - on paper things have worked out perfectly for Viktor Gyokeres since his Â£64m transfer to Arsenal.

But, even with those achievements, it has been a tough start to the current campaign for the 28-year-old striker.

The Swede has started just one Premier League game this season and is yet to score in his eight league appearances.

He has started three games in the Champions League, two in the Carabao Cup, and has scored just twice in 15 games in all competitions. Not the numbers he would have hoped for after last season's glory.

It is not just this season that has seen Gyokeres suitability questioned for Arsenal though.

Even though he scored more than 20 goals in his first season in all competitions as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait for a title, his all-round game had its critics.

It has been near enough a straight battle for the number nine role between Kai Havertz and Gyokeres since the Swedish international signed.

And Gyokeres was thrust into leading the line for Arsenal quicker and more frequently than planned after injury kept Havertz out for long periods last season.

Although the Swede may be the more natural finisher, Havertz's all-round play is considered superior with the German also one of Arteta's most trusted players for big games.

Gyokeres, a "win-now signing", was bought for his ability to find the net but also for how he could open up spaces for his team-mates, something they have praised him for.

But playing with his back to goal and linking up play is not natural to Gyokeres and his failure to hold up the ball or win duels with centre-backs has led to fan frustration.

Arteta has spoken about how the striker has been working on improving his hold-up play and connections, and there were hints of it in the Champions League win over Slavia Prague where Gyokeres assisted the opener and scored the winner in arguably his best game of the season.

Raya to miss Dortmund game but injury 'not serious'.

A big reason that Gyokeres is not starting games is that Havertz is fit.

Last season, Havertz suffered with knee and hamstring problems which meant Gyokeres was the only option Arteta had.

Had Havertz been fit, he would have played a lot more and the fact that he started the Champions League final and the key match away at Manchester City in last season's title race back this up.

This season Gyokeres has just six starts and Arteta says that his gametime and situation is similar to other members in the squad.

"We have rotated the team a lot and used the competitions as well to give minutes to players and exposure because they are all starters in my opinion," Arteta said.

"Viktor's case is one of many that they have been in the same situation where they play more in the Premier League or more in the Champions League which is not bad, eh?".

Arteta is open with his players about their standing in the squad and said that Gyokeres has not approached him directly about a lack of minutes.

"We have conversations with every player to make sure that they understand what we are doing and to gather information about the way we are feeling and so far it has been very positive with Viktor and the rest of the team," he remarked.

The signing of Gyokeres is an interesting one in its own right.

The Arsenal recruitment team had done a lot of due diligence on signing, now Manchester United forward, Benjamin Sesko.

It is understood work on that deal had been done but a change of direction to sign Gyokeres happened after Andrea Berta became Arsenal sporting director.

Some around Arsenal have always thought that Gyokeres is not the usual forward that the Gunners would go for and his predicament of a lack of game time was always likely to happen, even if he did play a big part in them ending their trophy drought.

Gyokeres ended last season with 14 league goals but those strikes actually only won Arsenal two points on their way to winning the league.

That is because, although his penalty in the 1-0 win at Everton was the only goal of the game, Arsenal would have come away with a draw, so that strike factually only accounted for two points and not three.

But Gyokeres did put the Gunners ahead five times last season in the league which shows that, among the frustrating performances, he had plenty of impact.

Max Dowman stole the show with his goal in the 2-0 home win over Everton, when he became the youngest scorer in Premier League history, but it was Gyokeres' goal in the 89th-minute which put Arsenal ahead and although it did not lead to a point score on its own, it set them on the way.

Gyokeres also scored in the 4-1 north London derby win, putting Arsenal ahead when Kolo Muani had equalised after Eberechi Eze's opener.

It is unlikely that Gyokeres will be sold in January as he continues to get games in the Champions League and is a senior player who can score goals in significant moments.

But if his lack of minutes in the league continue, Gyokeres, who is a driven and ambitious individual, will not want to be the player who is left out of the starting XI in the long term.

More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations.
  • In a recent development, A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a fresh explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries.
  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but latest research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

In a recent development, A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a fresh explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

Recent findings suggest that "Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he stated.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

Sources indicate that normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath newly introduced deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

It has been revealed that according to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

Sources indicate that the researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A Newly introduced Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

Recent findings suggest that this agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

Recent findings suggest that the research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

According to recent reports, materials provided by University of Wollongong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.
  • His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, revealed his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, revealed his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

It has been revealed that by the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

According to recent reports, by the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

It has been revealed that throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The Upcoming Yorker.

Sources indicate that T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is right now on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

  • This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall.
  • In a recent development, the satellite that rolled out with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night.

This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military introduced several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites.

In a recent development, the satellite that rolled out with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified.

Sources indicate that from its start, the Space Transportation System, better known as the space shuttle, was a compromise between meeting civilian and military needs. NASA saw the vehicle as a means of supporting science research, establishing an on-orbit economy (servicing commercial satellites and flying company payloads) and ultimately, assembling the parts for a space station.

Recent findings suggest that the Department of Defense saw the shuttle as an asset to deploying and retrieving reconnaissance satellites, among other projects, some of them classified. It was not until the loss of the space shuttle Challenger, that it was decided that the shuttle would only be used by the military when it was key to national security. Other needs would be met by expendable launch vehicles (ELVs).As an aside, the STS-33 astronauts also spent Thanksgiving in space during this mission. But the holiday was off to a crappy start when the shuttle's toilet broke first thing in the morning. After spending most of the day fixing it, they got to enjoy their Thanksgiving turkey together.

Recent findings suggest that want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

She presently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Aviation Administration remarked Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to matter a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have remarked L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.".

The agencies have mentioned they are working to figure out the root cause of the concern and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the newly introduced devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Recent findings suggest that duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, noted Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

Industry observers note that "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.".

Duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and noted it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The private jets are operated by Qatar Executive - a subsidiary of the Qatar Airways Group, which is one of Fifa's sponsors.

Fifa president Gianni Infantino's globetrotting by private jet since his initiative to sell off a stake in the World Cup can be revealed.

BBC Sport found Infantino has taken 39 private flights - the equivalent of one every three days - and visited 32 different countries since the news emerged on 28 July.

Our research found he travelled more than 102,800 air miles and spent just under nine days in the air in the space of 115 days.

Critics have accused of Infantino of using tools only at his disposal as president to aid his campaign for re-election next March.

They questioned whether his re-election campaign may have partly motivated any promises made or support offered during those visits.

Fifa said Infantino had a "statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations".

However, he visited nearly double the 18 countries he did in the same period in 2025.

The initial Times story that revealed Infantino's World Cup blueprint led to a wave of criticism around the world.

But, as BBC Sport revealed, many observers feel Infantino is now the favourite to be re-elected in the spring after his rivals struggled to find a candidate to run against him until the last moment.

And it appears Infantino has managed to shore up support around the world, with critics suggesting his globetrotting was a key part of that strategy.

There has also been concern about the environmental impact of his extensive travels.

Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - noted Infantino's travelling was "part of his campaign".

He told BBC Sport: "The issue here is that Fifa does not have rules on campaign funding, so the president can claim that he's going there on official business when indirectly he's using that to campaign.

"And anyone else running against him very likely will not have the financial means to compete with that.".

Infantino's position seemed vulnerable after it emerged he had been devising a plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, in a proposal called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

Before FFE was abandoned, Infantino wrote to all 211 member associations saying they would receive $40m (Â£30m) if they backed the plan.

Lars-Christer Olsson - a former chief executive of Uefa - told BBC Sport the "crucial" question was "what does he promise and what are the conditions, as he already did when he promised cash if the members supported his FFE project?".

BBC Sport gleaned the information about where Infantino had been travelling to, and when, from postings on his social media accounts.

The reasons for his travels include holding meetings with football association presidents, opening pitches, meeting politicians and attending confederation gatherings.

The private jets he used are operated by Qatar Executive (QE) - a subsidiary of the Qatar Airways Group, which is one of Fifa's sponsors.

BBC Sport used flight-tracking records and the jet registrations of the Qatar Executive fleet to compile a detailed log of Infantino's flights, totalling at least 39 since the start of August. Fifa did not dispute the figure.

It said "all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations" and there are "rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official".

But Fifa declined to comment on how the use of QE flights impacts on the money available from the Qatar Airways sponsorship for the benefit of global football.

The governing body also declined to comment when asked when Infantino had last taken a commercial flight.

Olsson said: "What do these trips cost and who is paying, which are the implications for the total football community?

"Is he provided with transport in his private campaign with the idea of getting something back in return if he is elected? If Fifa is paying for private jets, would it not be better to invest this money in the member associations?".

Maduro noted: "That's again a confusion between his role as president of Fifa and his role as candidate to Fifa presidency.".

He mentioned there were no regulations within Fifa on the "use of public money to support their campaign".

"There's no independent authority that controls that, there is no regulation of campaign funding," he remarked.

Infantino's trips included attending the Caribbean Football Union presidents' meeting and a junior football tournament in the Dominican Republic three weeks after FFE failed.

He then flew to Paris, where he attended the esports World Cup , alongside French President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman.

On his Instagram account, Infantino said he had "pledged Fifa's support" for the Pakistan Football Federation president's development intends when he met him in the US in September.

A few days later, he referenced a "wonderful discussion" with the president of the Latvian Football Federation during a visit to Riga, describing him as "my dear friend".

During a visit to Indonesia in October for the final of the Fifa ASEAN Cup, he met presidents from the football federations of Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, Maldives, Mongolia, Myanmar, Pakistan, Philippines, Qatar, Singapore, Thailand and Timor-Leste.

He said: "Having your support and shared passion on this momentous occasion means a great deal and together we will continue driving this game forward.".

And during a recent trip to Manila, he performed on stage as part of a quartet called the 'Backache Boys', alongside officials from the Asian Football Confederation, and the football federations of Malaysia and the Philippines.

Gianni Infantino opened a mini-pitch in Anguilla in November.

Gianni Infantino visited the Philippines for the ASEAN Football Federation Ordinary Congress.

Gianni Infantino in Qatar to oversee preparations for the Fifa U17 World Cup.

Based on our log of Infantino's private-jet flights, we calculated he spent 213 hours and 49 minutes in the air, travelling about 102,870 air miles.

For the type of private jet Infantino was using, this would produce an estimated 1,673 tonnes of CO2e emissions.

It has been revealed that that's equivalent to the emissions 252 people would accumulate on average in an entire year, according to European Union data, external. These figures are conservative estimates based on average fuel burn rates.

According to recent reports, fifa has also been criticised for expanding the number of teams at World Cups, and hosting them in multiple countries, thereby increasing the amount of travel. The 2026 World Cup was described as the 'most polluting World Cup ever'.

Freddie Daley, from the Cool Down Sport for Climate Action Network, said Infantino's behaviour was "emblematic of Fifa's approach to environmental sustainability under his leadership: total and utter disregard".

"Despite numerous pledges, Fifa has failed to deliver any significant proposal on how it will achieve them and has instead gone backwards," he added.

Maduro stated Fifa's support for initiatives on climate action - which included being a signatory of the United Nation's Sports for Climate Action Framework - was "window dressing".

Fifa did not directly respond to a question about its justification for the environmental impact caused by Infantino's extensive travelling.

A spokesperson for Fifa remarked its objectives were to "improve football constantly and promote it globally".

They added: "The Fifa president has a statutory duty to maintain and develop good relations between and among Fifa, the confederations, 211 member associations, political bodies, and international organisations.

According to recent reports, "To do that, he travels around the world and attends Fifa's tournaments and events. Mr Infantino is elected until 18 March 2027, when the next Fifa presidential election will take place.

"Fifa has put in place rules which establish the framework for flights and travel by any Fifa official.

"The Fifa president routinely travels around the world for various duties, together with relevant officials, on business and tournament-related matters and strives to visit member associations of Fifa whenever he can.

"Fifa expenses are published in our annual report, and all travel is in line with Fifa's regulations.

"Fifa's money belongs to the 211 member associations and an increased investment to $6.35bn for the upcoming cycle reinforces our unwavering commitment to further supporting football development and access globally.".

Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn.
  • A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.
  • It has been revealed that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

It has been revealed that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

Newly introduced Geological Clues Narrow the Search.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

According to recent reports, using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

It has been revealed that the scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:.

According to recent reports, "This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.".

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned.

Recent findings suggest that for generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, noted:.

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each upcoming piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.".

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the latest investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Industry observers note that stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

According to recent reports, if the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer notable clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:.

According to recent reports, "In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.".

The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed
