#162087. Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (877 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut.
  • In a recent development, the gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract.
  • According to recent reports, to investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.

In a recent development, the gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play vital roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the latest findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.

According to recent reports, to investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.

Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria.

In a recent development, the findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.

These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.

"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as vital as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," said Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.

This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone currently takes may overlook an important part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.

Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics.

One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.

Sources indicate that researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.

The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.

This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.

Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped.

To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.

By examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.

In a recent development, although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.

Recent findings suggest that selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.

Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought.

The findings point to an vital consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.

If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.

It has been revealed that the results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.

"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," noted Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.
  • While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.
  • In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.

While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.

In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

Sources indicate that NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency.

In a recent development, curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day, or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape.

In a recent development, data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.

Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity.

Back at Mount Sharp, Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock.

It has been revealed that the rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA.

By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons, researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain.

Together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater, both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • True to the Gijon Festival’s core focus on new talent, Mad Mengel, Jonas Spriestersbach and Claude Schmitz scored the main prizes at Gijón.
  • GIJÓN, Spain — “The Guest,” Mads Mengel’s directorial debut, has won the top Albar Award at the 64th Gijón/Xixón Film Festival.
  • Anthony Boyle and Yuki Katayama took the top acting prizes, while Félix De Givry (“Adieu monde cruel”) scored best director.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

True to the Gijon Festival’s core focus on new talent, Mad Mengel, Jonas Spriestersbach and Claude Schmitz scored the main prizes at Gijón.

GIJÓN, Spain — “The Guest,” Mads Mengel’s directorial debut, has won the top Albar Award at the 64th Gijón/Xixón Film Festival.

Anthony Boyle and Yuki Katayama took the top acting prizes, while Félix De Givry (“Adieu monde cruel”) scored best director.

Danish feature “The Guest”, which premiered at Karlovy Vary, marks out Mengel as a “director to watch,” explained FICX director Alejandro Díaz Castaño at the closing ceremony. Related Stories Chris Pratt to Continue 'Terminal List' Story in 'Savage Son' Series for Amazon Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade at 100: Massive Minions, K-Pop Stars and ‘Sorcerer’s Apprentice’ Mickey Mouse.

The feature is a family drama centering on a troubled mother-son relationship and a simple family gathering that fast derails.

Variety’s reviewer Jessica Kiang wrote, “A droll dramedy of bourgeois social awkwardness morphs into a deep-cut tragedy about the effects of a mother’s psychological frailty on her grown-up children, in Danish director Mads Mengel‘s impressively uncozy debut.”.

Yuki Katayama scooped the best AISGE actress award for her performance in Japan’s “Fujiko,” from Taichi Kimura), playing a single-mother facing the challenge of singly raising a child.

Irish actor Anthony Boyle nabbed the best actor award for his turn in Clio Barnard’s “I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning,” a story of five friends growing up and the importance of both family and friendships.

The 64th FICX honorary prize was shared between two cult figures at the festival: Irish actor, writer and director Peter Mullan while a special mention went to Mexican-director Carlos Reygadas.

Mullan has a long standing relationship with Gijón after working as an actor with Ken Loach, Danny Boyle and Steven Spielberg among other. He won 1998’s Gijón Festival top prize for his directorial debut, “Orphans.” Since then, as a director, he was awarded a Venice Golden Lion back in 2002 for “The Magdalene Sisters”) and San Sebastián Golden Shell in 2010 for “Neds.”.

Almost 20 years have passed since Reygadas’ received a retrospective back in 2007 when he won a 2007 Cannes Jury Prize for “Silent Light.” He then won Cannes’ 2012 best director award for “Post Tenebras Lux.” The festival’s relationship with Reygadas underscores its core passion and value of following and promoting talent. Reygadas also competed at Albar this edition with his latest feature “Heil Jupiter!”.

Special mention was made to a well-known figure of the festival, former Gijón Festival director José Luis Cienfuegos (1995-2011), who passed away last year.

Packed theaters and record-breaking ticket sales at Gijón this year ratified its art-house selection.

“Filmmakers who have been here feel how we take care of them and their projects as part of the community and that creates a pull effect that brings talent to the festival,” explained Diaz Castaño.

Recent findings suggest that in other awards, Claude Schmitz’s Belgian-French “Conrad & Crab” won the FICX Premiere Award, its jury justifying the prize for the way in the film fiction blends into reality in a spirit compared to Chaplin and Kaurismäki. In the same section, Agathe Bonitzer’s “Journal du Futur” took an artistic contribution award for her debut, an original documentary built from images she has recorded since she was 15.

The Fipresci best feature award went to Jonas Spriestersbach’s “Meanwhile in Namibia.” The jury praised its “discreet, non-didactic and at times humorous approach to how historical atrocities still resonate today” calling it a film that captures the true spirit of independent cinema, as it was made on a highly contained budget.

In a recent development, the award resonates with the true identity of not only the festival, but its partners as well and adds to Spriestersbach’s success with Warsaw festival’s Documentary & Audience Award and a German Film Award at Dok.fest Munich. The feature explores Namibia’s evolution since German colonial rule and its recent territorial disputes with its neighbors.

Sources indicate that ana Urushadze’s “Supporting Role,” a Georgia-Estonia-Turkey-Switzerland-U.S. co-production, proved a double winner, taking both the Youth Jury prize for best Retueyos feature and the CIMA Award for best feature film directed by a woman. The juries highlighted its depth, immersiveness, cinematography and performances.

Following an aging Georgian film star, the film becomes a nocturnal odyssey through Tbilisi. It took the Fipresci Award at Rotterdam and Urushadze, while scoring the Heart of Sarajevo best director award.

Xisi Sofia Ye Chen walked off with both best Spanish feature and the RC Service award for best director with France-Spain co-production, “From Dawn to Dawn.”.

It has been revealed that the feature of the rising Chinese-Spanish director follows her brother, a Chinese gangster living in Spain, and portrays her family’s evolution and reconciliation with its own past. The feature also scored 2026’s Vision Du Réel Grand Jury Prize.

Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier won the scriptwriters association’s DAMA best screenplay award for their Swiss-Spanish debut, “Les Indes.” The unconventional film combines images, the arrival of colonialism and forgotten voices of ordinary people.

Industry observers note that david Hernández and Alex Penabade’s “Anxo” took AMAE’s editing award. Set in Galicia, in northwest Spain, the film follows a 1972 workers’ strike that happened at Vigo’s shipyards, where workers demanded better conditions and clashes with police escalated as the strike dragged on.

It has been revealed that tesla owners know all about subscription pricing when it comes to their vehicles. The organization's Tesla Full Self-Driving (Supervised) feature requires a subscription of $99 per month.

Of course, Tesla owners don't need FSD in order to drive their vehicles. They can drive the car that they own without paying the monthly fee. But what if a subscription was required?

That's the case with Tesla's latest Cybercab.

Recent findings suggest that in order to use the $29,990 Cybercab at all, owners will be required to pay $299 per month for a subscription. Without the subscription, the Cybercab won't move.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk did share on his social media platform X that he thought the subscription was too pricey.

"The monthly fee is too high," Musk posted. "Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month." It should be noted that the monthly fee can change at any time. And while Musk mentioned he'd like to lower the price, Tesla could also raise it.

In addition to the required $299-a-month subscription just to use the Cybercab, there are other restrictive terms that buyers must agree to.

Sources indicate that for example, Cybercab owners cannot put wraps on their vehicle, tint the windows, or change the wheels unless the work is approved by and done through Tesla. If owners make those changes without Tesla, the organization can suspend a Cybercab owner's subscription, effectively bricking their car.

In addition, subscriptions can be temporarily suspended without refund if a Cybercab owner operates the vehicle in an improper or unsafe manner.

Sources indicate that another rule, at least for now, is that a Cybercab can only be used for personal use. Tesla Cybercabs cannot be used for rentals or with apps like Uber or DoorDash.

It has been revealed that the Tesla Cybercab is also geofenced, meaning it currently can only be used in approved areas of Texas. Attempting to use the car outside of the approved areas can result in operation of the vehicle being "technologically prevented.".

#162081. Tech Report: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1612 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object.
  • According to recent reports, scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission.
  • The telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an notable milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.

According to recent reports, scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.

The telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.

With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.

A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years.

For its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.

By examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.

Sources indicate that the main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.

One crucial measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.

That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.

Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space.

Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.

Professor Bunce said: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is new!

Recent findings suggest that "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.

"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase.".

The results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.

The team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector highlights no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.

Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.

How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry.

Industry observers note that bepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.

Sources indicate that one of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.

Sources indicate that MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.

According to recent reports, it is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.

Recent findings suggest that the instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.

MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.

Industry observers note that the telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal notable connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.

A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy.

For Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.

Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.

Dr. Martindale said: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was rolled out.

Recent findings suggest that "This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit.".

Recent findings suggest that the milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.

Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations.".

BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury.

BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.

The remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.

Industry observers note that the mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.

For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.

International Collaboration and Funding.

MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:.

UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An audiovisual co-production treaty between India and Chile has reached the last stage of negotiation, according to Jorge Loyola Castro, Chile’s trade commissioner to India, who spoke to Variety at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

The talks trace back to then-President Gabriel Boric’s state visit to India in April 2025, the first by a Chilean president since Michelle Bachelet’s trip in 2009. Castro indicates the visit set the co-production negotiations in motion. In a joint statement issued during the trip, Boric and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi named audiovisual co-production among the areas where the two countries would look to work together. José Antonio Kast succeeded Boric as president in March. Related Stories Hollywood's Next Big Deal: Will Netflix Make an M&A Play for NBCU? Why 'Suits' Japan Swapped Drugs for Cash: NBCUniversal, TBS Format Chiefs on Localizing Hits at Taiwan Creative Content Fest.

“It has been started and now is at the final, final stage, so we hope that we can bring some news soon,” Loyola tells Variety.

There is no firm date yet. Loyola points out that the process only began last year, adding: “We really, really hope that by next year we can announce something. If something happens earlier, more than happy, but it’s a priority for Chile as well.”.

It has been revealed that the treaty is moving alongside a broader trade pact, the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement. The two sides finalized its terms of reference during Boric’s visit and have held four rounds of talks since, the most recent in Fresh Delhi in December 2025, according to India’s embassy in Santiago. India’s commerce secretary traveled to Chile in August to advance the negotiations. Bilateral trade grew from $3.84 billion in 2024 to $5.38 billion in 2025, with Indian imports of Chilean gold accounting for much of the rise.

Chilean producers are already lining up. Giancarlo Nasi, producer and CEO of Quijote Films, which operates out of Santiago and Los Angeles, came off a strong 2025. Quijote produced Diego Céspedes’ “The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo,” winner of the Un Certain Regard prize at Cannes, and co-produced Gabriel Mascaro’s Brazilian drama “The Blue Trail,” which took the Grand Jury Prize in Berlin.

Industry observers note that “I love pushing the boundaries of what is possible and doing the craziest co-production that you can find. So co-producing with India would be ideal,” Nasi notes.

Without a treaty, Quijote gets around the gap by bringing in a partner from a third country that has a treaty with Chile. A French company on Ukrainian drama “Pamfir,” which played Cannes in 2022, allowed Quijote to tap the Chilean-French treaty. A French company was also attached early on to John Trengove’s South African drama “The Smell of Apples,” which premiered at Toronto in September, and a French producer is on board the documentary Quijote is now making with Moroccan filmmaker Asmae El Moudir, who shared Cannes’ documentary prize for “The Mother of All Lies” in 2023.

Sources indicate that A direct treaty would remove that detour. Nasi says the key is for Chile to build “a minoritarian co-production fund that is bigger and bigger and stronger so it can actually make a difference for an Indian production.”.

A fan of Indian cinema since childhood, Nasi cites “RRR” and “The Lunchbox” as proof of its range. He has been receiving Indian projects, but has yet to find the right one. Many come from Indian filmmakers living in the U.S. who want to tell stories of migration and return, often on mid-sized budgets with no state funding available to them. He would like to make a film that spans India, the U.S. and Chile.

“There’s a crisis in the States in terms of financing independent movies because the distribution system of independent movies is changing,” Nasi indicates. “Theaters are more and more reserved to horror genre movies or substantial movies, so the independent dramas, they’re having trouble finding a place.”.

Industry observers note that chile’s factual sector is also in the hunt. Miguel Soffia, founder and director of Santiago-based We Are South, who has spent 15 years producing factual content with streamers and broadcasters around the world, is drawing up deal memos and contracts with a company he met at the market that is behind a hornbill film. The project is a natural history co-production about massive cats – the puma, the snow leopard and the Eurasian lynx – spanning India, the Andes and Europe.

Recent findings suggest that “We ran into a company here that was brilliant. They were doing the same stuff as us and it was just serendipity,” Soffia says.

It has been revealed that the project follows “Extremes of the Americas,” a six-part series on climate change that We Are South co-produced with Canada and shot in northern Canada and southern Chile. Soffia is also developing a Pacific Ring of Fire project connecting Japan, the Philippines, Tahiti and New Zealand with the Americas through earthquakes, tsunamis and volcanoes, and has a potential Canadian co-producer at the market.

Sources indicate that talking to Malaysian contacts, Soffia found that they share myths with Indigenous communities back home, in which oxen cause earthquakes in a struggle between land and sea. “Of course, there’s a science basis to it, but there’s also a massive cultural phenomenon and human experience in common that we want to explore in that film,” he indicates.

As for Quijote’s next step once a treaty is signed: “Do a lot of Indian movies,” Nasi claims.

  • The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever.

Sources indicate that after launching the Fresh Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground. This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history.

The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.

It has been revealed that today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms.

But in the end, Blue Origin did it first.

Blue Origin's New Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket.

Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with Upcoming Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company declared a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects.

But Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the tech giant's success with Newly introduced Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown.

Blue Origin has since reflown a Latest Glenn booster, and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance.

Latest Update: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
  • Sources indicate that the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m.
  • The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years of traveling through space, humanity's most distant spacecraft is now approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from home. At that distance, even a signal moving at the speed of light needs an entire day to make the journey.

Sources indicate that the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST). Scientists and engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone.

The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.

Voyager 1 Is Now 24 Light-Hours From Earth.

Recent findings suggest that astronomers often describe enormous cosmic distances in terms of how long light takes to travel them. A light-day represents the distance light covers in 24 hours, or roughly 16.1 billion miles.

Industry observers note that light moves through a vacuum at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second. To put Voyager 1's distance in perspective, sunlight passing Earth takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Reaching Neptune takes roughly four hours, while traveling from Neptune to Voyager 1 requires another 20 hours.

According to recent reports, even these enormous distances are small compared with those separating stars. A single light-year, the distance light travels in one year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1's extraordinary distance also creates a major challenge for mission controllers. Sending a command to the spacecraft now requires 24 hours, and receiving a response takes another 24 hours. A complete exchange therefore spans two full days, even though the signals travel at the fastest speed possible.

According to recent reports, the milestone comes as engineers investigate a communication problem. NASA has not received scientific or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. However, the probe continues transmitting a carrier signal, the radio signal that normally carries information back to Earth. By tracking this signal and calculating the spacecraft's trajectory, mission specialists were able to verify that Voyager 1 had crossed the one light-day mark. Engineers are continuing to investigate why the expected data is not coming through.

A Historic Journey Beyond the Solar System's Planets.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, were launched in 1977 to take advantage of an unusual arrangement of the outer planets. The alignment allowed the spacecraft to use planetary gravity to travel from one destination to another, making an ambitious exploration mission possible.

Managed by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these distant planets, revealing extraordinary new details about their atmospheres, rings, and moons. Voyager 2 continued farther, becoming the first spacecraft to explore Uranus and Neptune up close.

Sources indicate that today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them humanity's only spacecraft to have crossed into the region beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring changes in the Sun's magnetic field across immense distances, providing scientists with measurements that cannot be collected from Earth.

"Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets," mentioned Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "But it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.".

It has been revealed that "Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. "Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.".

Voyager's Golden Record Carries a Message From Earth.

The Voyager spacecraft carry more than scientific instruments. Each also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. These recordings were designed as messages that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might discover someday.

The records give the mission a purpose extending far beyond its scientific discoveries. Even after the spacecraft eventually lose the ability to communicate with Earth, they will continue traveling through space with a small collection of sights and sounds from the planet that introduced them.

According to recent reports, "Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward," mentioned Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. "Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.".

Exploring the Mysterious Region Beyond the Sun.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 1 is right now moving through space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, a vast region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

This protective bubble helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, where particles and magnetic fields from the broader galaxy become more dominant.

Voyager 2 followed a different route and crossed into interstellar space in 2018. Together, the probes are providing the first direct observations of conditions beyond the heliosphere.

One of their most intriguing discoveries is that the Sun's effects do not simply disappear at the boundary. Its influence appears to extend much farther into interstellar space than scientists once understood, raising new questions about where the environment shaped by our star truly gives way to the surrounding galaxy.

"The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere," said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. "One significant surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.".

How NASA Is Keeping Voyager 1 Alive After Nearly 50 Years.

Operating spacecraft built nearly half a century ago requires increasingly inventive engineering. Both Voyagers have experienced problems as their equipment ages, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer. NASA engineers have repeatedly developed solutions that allow the probes to continue working despite these setbacks.

In a recent development, electricity has become one of the mission's greatest limitations. Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by switching off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing them with three alternatives that consume less power. This change was intended to help the spacecraft stretch its remaining energy supply.

Voyager 1 depends on a radioisotope thermal generator that is now approximately 50 years old. Often described as a nuclear battery, the device produces electricity by converting heat released during the radioactive decay of plutonium.

According to recent reports, as the radioactive material continues to decay, the available power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately four watts of electrical output every year, forcing engineers to make difficult decisions about which systems can remain operational.

The latest conservation measures are expected to provide enough power to operate the spacecraft's current scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when both probes will celebrate their 50th launch anniversaries.

One Day, Voyager 1 Will Become a Silent Messenger to the Stars.

Industry observers note that maintaining contact across such staggering distances requires some of NASA's most powerful communications equipment. The agency relies on its Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of large radio antennas located at three facilities, to communicate with Voyager and other spacecraft traveling to and beyond the Moon.

Despite the enormous communication delay and the spacecraft's aging systems, engineers continue monitoring Voyager 1 daily and transmitting instructions every week. The mission remains an extraordinary demonstration of what long-term spacecraft engineering can achieve.

According to recent reports, "We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," mentioned Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. "Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars.".

The International Emmy Awards, the global version of the U.S. TV honors, were handed out in Fresh York Monday night.

Industry observers note that the top prize of best drama went to French foodie-themed period series Carême from Apple TV. The series beat out Steven Knight’s Hulu boxing drama A Thousand Blows; Prime Video’s Argentine political drama Menem; and underdog sports drama Real Kashmir Football Club from Indian pay-TV group Sony LIV.

North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
  • But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
  • That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.

But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.

That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.

It has been revealed that "The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa mentioned ahead of the meeting.

North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.

But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Proposal.

However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on.".

Kos stated that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.

For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.

Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.

Recent findings suggest that bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.

The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.

From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.

According to recent reports, "It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.

North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.

EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.

Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.

President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova claims North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.

"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she noted.

After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.

It has been revealed that A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.

Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession at the moment required to move forward.

That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.

The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.

The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.

For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.

The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.

In a recent development, the uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.

According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.

"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

#162072. A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1818 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it.
  • Researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger.
  • Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a new lease on life.

Researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

Recent findings suggest that "Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a fresh paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.".

How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion.

For thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.

The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

"We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!".

Industry observers note that scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

Recent findings suggest that "When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," stated co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in New York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.".

A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome.

In a recent development, this kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.

As the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.

Recent findings suggest that for Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.

But such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

In a recent development, these surviving systems are key because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.

Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.

Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb.

To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

The simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.

Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Massive Bao.".

"It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," mentioned co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.

At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.

Sources indicate that further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.

Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De stated.

The merger has left astronomers with another important question: What is Bao like now?

According to recent reports, the surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.

Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs.

One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

Sources indicate that although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.

The researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.).

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.

In a recent development, earlier records highlighted that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) highlighted further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another important development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

It has been revealed that the telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.

Sources indicate that then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

According to recent reports, scientists promptly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable latest measurements.

Webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.

A New Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars.

The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an crucial advance in the study of stellar mergers.

Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

That timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.

The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.

NASA's recently rolled out Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

In a recent development, one of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.

With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar stated.

The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

The James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.

Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • More than two decades after its release, the singer-songwriter's 2003 breakup anthem "Are You Happy Now?" is finding a new audience on TikTok, thanks to a particularly memorable needle drop in Netflix's buzzy teen horror drama The Body.
  • Welcome to the Michelle Branch renaissance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michelle Branch has a question for Gen Z: Are you happy now?

More than two decades after its release, the singer-songwriter's 2003 breakup anthem "Are You Happy Now?" is finding a new audience on TikTok, thanks to a particularly memorable needle drop in Netflix's buzzy teen horror drama The Body. And for millennials who grew up screaming along to the song in their bedrooms, the sudden resurgence feels like a long-overdue moment of recognition — and another painful reminder that we're all old AF.

Welcome to the Michelle Branch renaissance. We've been expecting you.

It has been revealed that the song appears in the third episode of The Body, a psychological horror series set at a Catholic girls' school in 2004, where a dance team initiation spirals into a supernatural panic. The show's early-aughts setting provides plenty of opportunities for nostalgic needle drops, with a soundtrack featuring Kelly Clarkson, Ciara, Kylie Minogue, and No Doubt. But Branch's angsty pop-rock hit gets one of the show's most memorable musical moments.

During a church service, Elise puts on a convincing display of demonic possession, collapsing as the song builds toward its explosive chorus. The juxtaposition of religious imagery, teenage hysteria, and Branch's soaring vocals makes for a scene practically engineered to go viral.

And that's exactly what's happening on social media.

Industry observers note that originally released in 2003 as the lead single from Branch's supremely underrated sophomore album, Hotel Paper, "Are You Happy Now?" became one of the defining songs of the early-2000s pop-rock boom. With its crunchy guitars, emotionally charged vocals, and deliciously confrontational chorus, the track captured a particular kind of teenage heartbreak — the kind that demands to be felt at full volume.

In a recent development, it was a time when young women like Branch, Avril Lavigne, and Vanessa Carlton were helping shape the sound of mainstream pop, bringing guitars, messy emotions, and confessional songwriting to a generation of listeners. They embraced teenage melodrama, not shied away from it.

Now, more than 20 years later, that sound is resonating with a new generation. Just look at the comments on the song's YouTube music video, where the top comment asks, "Who's here after The Body?".

On TikTok, younger listeners are discovering the cathartic power of Branch's early-aughts angst. One user declared it the new background song to their life, while another thanked The Body for introducing them to this "cunty asf song." Others are already looking to expand their musical horizons. "I've been obsessed with this song since The Body," one user wrote, asking for recommendations for artists with a similar sound.

According to recent reports, but the nostalgia goes beyond the music itself. One TikToker lamented being born in 2004 instead of getting to experience the year as a teenager, adding, "God I'm SO jealous of millennials." Another praised the show's music supervisor with a particularly heartfelt blessing: "Whoever put this soundtrack together, I hope both sides of your pillow are cold cause wow, you get it.".

The resurgence is part of a familiar pattern in which television and social media introduce younger audiences to older music. Kate Bush's "Running Up That Hill" famously experienced a massive revival after appearing in Stranger Things, while TikTok has repeatedly turned decades-old tracks into contemporary hits.

Industry observers note that what makes "Are You Happy Now?" particularly well-suited to this moment is that its emotional intensity never really went out of style. The song's combination of wounded pride, anger, and catharsis translates just as easily to a TikTok edit as it did to a burned CD in 2003.

For Gen Z, it might be a fresh discovery. For millennials, it's confirmation of something we've known all along: Michelle Branch was always that girl.

In a recent development, for a generation that grew up online, the early 2000s have become something of a cultural fantasy. From Y2K fashion and digital cameras to wired headphones and the resurgence of pop-rock, Gen Z has embraced the aesthetics of a time when the internet still seemed full of possibility. More recently, the "millennial optimism" trend has romanticized the late 2000s and early 2010s, when Tumblr aesthetics, twee fashion, and earnest indie music dominated the internet. It's quite the turnaround for a generation that once made mocking millennial cringe something of a pastime.

But millennial optimism is about more than nostalgia for a particular aesthetic. It's a longing for a time when the future seemed brighter, when hope and sincerity felt less embarrassing, and when pop culture wasn't quite so steeped in irony. Of course, the past wasn't nearly as carefree as nostalgia might suggest. Still, there's something appealing about the emotional earnestness of that era, especially its music.

And while "Are You Happy Now?" might not exactly embody millennial optimism, its resurgence taps into that same longing for a seemingly simpler cultural moment. The platforms might have changed how we discover music, but the desire to scream along to a song that understands exactly how you feel hasn't changed much at all.

Next up: Justice for Carlton's "White Houses.".

#162067. Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
